newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asian petrochemical demand draws naphtha east.
newsitem.headline: Asian petrochemical demand draws naphtha east.

text.p: Asia's thirst for naptha, the petrochemical feedstock, is starting to have a global impact with high prices attracting Mediterranean cargoes for the first time since the Gulf War, industry sources said on Tuesday.

"Asia has been at the end of the whip for a long time. It is now at the whip handle ... a small swing in the whip handle creates big cracks at the end," said Bud Moeller, managing director of the Asia-Pacific energy and chemical practice of Booz-Allen and Hamilton Management Consultants.
The naptha deficit in the Asia-Pacific region is likely to grow to 488,000 barrels per day (bpd) this year from 417,000 bpd in 1994, according to Hawaii's East-West Center.
As a key feedstock in petrochemical production, naphtha is processed through an aromatics or ethylene plant in the manufacture of plastics, polyesters and synthethic rubber.
Fuelling the growth in naphtha demand is a series of new plants mainly in Singapore, Thailand, Indonesia and India.
On Monday, India's Reliance commissioned a 750,000 tonne-per-year ethylene plant, the largest naphtha cracker in Asia.
By 2000, Thailand plans to add 1.9 million tonnes of ethylene capacity to become Southeast Asia's largest producer, at 3.0 million tonnes a year.
A 650,000 tonne-per-year aromatics plant was commissioned in December and a 350,000 tonne-per-year ethylene plant started earlier this month.
Singapore also plans to become a regional petrochemical hub and naphtha exports from Asia's export-orientated refining centre are evaporating.
In January, an aromatics plant requiring 1.5 million tonnes of naphtha a year started up. In April, a 515,000 tonne-per-year ethylene plant will be commissioned.
Earlier this month, Exxon Chemicals decided to go ahead with plans to build a 800,000 tonne-per-year plant in Singapore by 2000.
But Mobil Corp is still mulling a project of similar size in Singapore amid increasing competition in the region.
"In the past five to 10 years, people were looking hungrily at projects in Asia with its high growth environment. But the road from yesterday to the future has many bumps," Moeller said.

"The reality is everyone in Asia is dancing around the equation of demand and capacity, but no one wants to be last. If two or three companies make the same move to build, it exacerbates the lumpiness," he said.

The recent rush of new plants has pushed naphtha prices in Asia much higher than in the West and traders were shipping around 200,000 tonnes of naphtha into Asia, mainly from the Mediterranean, for arrival in April and May.
Traders said these cargoes have already been sold and naptha should keep flowing into Asia as long as the East-West price differential remained greater than the freight costs of around $25 per tonne.
"One of the reasons for cargoes moving here suddenly is because the West is so weak," said a trader at a European major oil company.
"Especially last year, it was completely the opposite situation. But the bubble has burst and cargoes are flooding to this side because of strong demand," he said.
